codex.worst_flaw: The safety audit uses job records alone, so technicians could earn the reward for timely submissions while skipping physical checks or leaving hazards undocumented.

claude.worst_flaw: The crew-level staggered comparison has no stated sample size, uncertainty handling or predefined cost/harm decision rule. With only two groups drawn from about 300 technicians, crew case mix and spillover could easily overwhelm the reward effect, so the result may not show what the reward adds on top of the workflow fixes.

holistic.reason: Union-friendly, workflow-first design with a staggered pilot, clear metrics and anti-gaming safeguards is highly approvable, but a one-hour paid-time reward is modest and fixed two-week windows may leave limited salience, while durability depends mostly on whether the workflow fixes stick.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward pilot is blocked until it can validate actual work-start times, because reviewing the same job records used to award credit can miss technicians who start work before completing the checklist.

claude.worst_flaw: The quality audit relies on a 10-record weekly sample, which cannot reliably catch checklists ticked through without a real inspection or pressure to log holds, and there is no independent validation of the counting logic and no event history that can be replayed.

holistic.reason: It fixes the workflow before rewarding, gives a fair self-referenced goal, protects union interests, and pairs a randomized stagger with guardrails and clear stop rules, but one paid hour is a modest incentive and the fairness and sampling details add some complexity.

claude.worst_flaw: Learning design compares two stepped-wedge waves over only two weeks, with no sample size, uncertainty handling, spillover control, or predefined cost and harm outcomes. Its single follow-up metric also cannot detect quality degradation or safety incidents.

codex.worst_flaw: The same paid hour requires 100% completion from a technician with five eligible visits and 25% from one with twenty.

holistic.reason: Union co-design, private goals, hold-equals-completion credit, a staggered-wave design with a pre-agreed decision rule and a random audit make it approvable, but the five-visit goal over two weeks and a single paid hour are modest, and the checklist is only the default step, so a rise in completion may fade once credits stop.

claude.worst_flaw: The design never says who can see per-reviewer timestamps or the raw records behind the private progress messages. Event and policy versions can't be replayed, nothing independently checks the counts before launch beyond a few edge-case tests, and the only route for correcting a count goes privately to the rota owner, so there's no staffed, transparent appeal.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot cannot reliably isolate the paid hour’s effect because reviewers share PRs across groups and the reward windows occur at different times.

holistic.reason: The workflow fixes (rota, queue, protected time) and the explicit exit criteria suit sceptical engineers and should help, but the proposal is intricate and its one-paid-hour reward is small and tightly rule-bound. Many engineers may barely register it, and the gains depend on the workflow changes sticking after the reward ends.

codex.worst_flaw: The post-pilot decision uses timeliness alone, so the team could keep a workflow that reaches 90% while review quality declines.

claude.worst_flaw: Credit counting relies on the code host alone, with no replayable event or policy versioning, no independent shadow validation of the tally and no staffed appeal route beyond the owner correcting disputes privately. The within-group before/during/after comparison also cannot separate the reward from time trends or from spillover between groups that share reviewers.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, with sceptic-friendly private tallies, co-design, a staggered rollout and quality sampling, but one hour of PTO is a small reward, the programme is fairly complex to run, and lasting change depends on the retained routing and protected time rather than on the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: The decision rule says to pool weeks 3–4 "after the prizes end", but weeks 3–4 are reward weeks, and the design never sets a post-payout follow-up window. That leaves the persistence and stop decisions without valid measurement.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot has no decision rule for whether the paid-time-off reward earns its cost, and differences in case mix or spillover between rotations could distort the estimated benefit.

holistic.reason: The design fixes the actual bottleneck (routing, coverage, protected time) before rewarding, uses a modest private reward with a staggered comparison and anti-gaming checks, which suits sceptical engineers, but it is detailed and administratively heavy, the one-hour prize is small, and the rewards end at week 6 so lasting change depends on the workflow defaults sticking.

codex.worst_flaw: The decision to retain kiosk logging relies on unvalidated matching between anonymous entries and observed actions, so concurrent activity or safely deferred logging can distort the adoption rate.

claude.worst_flaw: The kiosk measures documentation, not hand hygiene, and the design never says what clinical or infection-control value the logging adds to the existing observer audits, so the 80% coverage target may not justify the time it costs nurses.

holistic.reason: Well-designed, safety-conscious pilot with fixed-workflow-first, no individual rewards, clear stop rules and honest measurement, but recognition is modest and complex, so nurse motivation and post-recognition habit retention are uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: The reward counts self-reported shift records as complete without verifying that they cover eligible hand-hygiene moments, so the pilot could mistake box-ticking for better documentation.

claude.worst_flaw: The reward pays for a 'complete' self-reported record, defined vaguely as 'the moments the nurse can reliably report', and nothing checks those entries against real care moments: weekly checks only test internal consistency, and the monthly observer audit is ward-level and too coarse to catch fabricated or retrospective logging.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with co-design, privacy, staggered rollout, independent audit and clear stop rules, but it is complex and rewards documentation rather than hygiene itself, and 30 minutes of time off is a modest incentive that may not sustain logging once it ends.

claude.worst_flaw: The design rewards and tracks only kiosk logging (one first record, then the share of shifts with an entry), so it never tests whether logging improves the observer-measured hand-hygiene compliance it is supposed to serve. It also has no replayable audit trail or appeal that is independent of the verifying educator.

codex.worst_flaw: The primary adoption measure is invalid for deciding whether to retain the kiosk because one valid entry can make an entire shift count as adopted even when most eligible hand-hygiene moments go undocumented.

holistic.reason: It is a cautious, well-governed pilot with privacy, pause triggers, a staggered rollout and pre-set thresholds, but it is complex, rewards only a single logged case, and relies on the educator for verification, so awareness and long-term habit are uncertain.

codex.worst_flaw: The pilot is not launchable as specified because valid exception notes alone could meet the 40% success threshold even if relevant article links and approved articles never increase.

claude.worst_flaw: The valid-exception path has no explicit cap or per-agent exception-rate trigger beyond a 12-ticket weekly sample (about 0.2 tickets per agent), so agents could hit their targets with boilerplate exceptions, and the team-level comparison with no stated sample size may be underpowered to detect it.

holistic.reason: Fixes the workflow friction first, rewards a correct outcome with valid exceptions, uses a randomized staggered rollout, audits for gaming and watches CSAT, and sets a pre-committed decision rule, though a one-hour reward is modest and the personalized targets and manual confirmation add some complexity.

codex.worst_flaw: The staggered pilot specifies neither how teams are assigned to each wave nor how uncertainty will be assessed, so differences in queues or timing could be mistaken for an effect of the reward.

claude.worst_flaw: Missing a two-week target means the agent cannot earn the reward at all, with no next chance. Corrections go only to the coordinator who also runs the audit, with no event or policy history and no independent appeal. The staggered comparison has no planned sample size or uncertainty handling, and it ignores spillover between teams.

holistic.reason: Well-designed with private feedback, pilot testing, fraud checks, staggered rollout and a clear decision metric, but a one-hour PTO reward for a two-week window is modest and may go unnoticed, and the habit may fade once the reward and tracking end, even though the workflow change itself is built into closeout.

codex.worst_flaw: An agent can earn the full reward through exceptions alone, so meeting the personal goal can contribute zero useful articles to the programme’s primary outcome.

claude.worst_flaw: The 'useful article' judgment and the 'valid exception' category rest on one coordinator's discretion. There is no replayable event or policy history, no independent shadow validation and no staffed appeal path, so both credit and the decision metric could drift or be gamed through exceptions. The pilot also randomizes only a few existing teams over a two-week window, with no stated sample size or uncertainty handling.

holistic.reason: Well-designed pilot with workflow fixes, audits, randomized comparison and CSAT safeguards, but the exception route and the complexity of the rules invite gaming and confusion, and one hour off for five tickets may not shift habits once it ends.
